docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Autonomous Mobile Robots Bootcamp Qualifier is a self-paced, free preparatory program consisting of instructional videos and hands-on programming exercises.

Students who successfully complete the qualifier will be considered for an invitation to the Autonomous Mobile Robots Bootcamp. In order to qualify you have to email solutions to (see Submissions tab) pranav@uic.edu.

The qualifier requires 10–20 hours depending on past experience with Python and using LLMs. You can expect to complete it in 1 to 2 weeks at 10 hours per week.

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
At the end of these exercises, students will be able to:

  1. Apply Python programming techniques to create scientific visualizations and animations.
  2. Configure and use Python libraries such as NumPy and Matplotlib for computations.
  3. Navigate and operate the MuJoCo robotics simulation environment.
  4. Model robotic systems and design controllers for simulation-based experiments in MuJoCo.
  5. Create interactive robotic simulations and games using MuJoCo.

docs.title: Equipment list
docs.text:
All the resources are free.

  1. Microsoft Visual Studio Code for Python: Download and install from here: Microsoft Visual Studio Code. Set up Python using this video and test a simple script shown in the video: https://youtu.be/9o4gDQvVkLU.

  2. Install additional Python packages: Packages can be installed by typing the following in the "terminal" in Microsoft Visual Studio Code:

    python3 -m pip install {package_name}

    You need to run this command for each package. For {package_name}, type numpy and matplotlib. This minute-long video shows how to install a package: https://youtu.be/sQPgR1Fz67c. 3. Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo): Install the Python package for MuJoCo by typing in the "terminal" inside Visual Studio Code:

    python3 -m pip install mujoco
    4. AI tools (highly recommended): Feel free to use AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, etc. You can also search and copy-paste code from other sources like GitHub or Stack Exchange. My general advice is to outline a method for solving the problem and use these tools to help you code. You do not need to buy a premium version of AI tools — just use the free one. The bootcamp is based on extensively using AI tools to code and debug.

docs.text:
If you have any questions, or run into any issues with these instructions — including dead links — feel free to email pranav@uic.edu.

Continue to Part 1: Introduction to Python.

docs.title: Part 1: Introduction to Python
docs.text: For this section, you will need to install Microsoft Visual Studio Code and the numpy and matplotlib packages (see items 1 and 2 in the Equipment list).

docs.title: 1.1 Basics of Python (~2 hours)
docs.text:
Material: Watch the video and practise coding as you watch it.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yutMT6NbjOU

All the code is also available for download here: Lec01_python_basics.zip

Exercises: After solving these problems, create a single zipped folder called 1a_basics.zip containing all Python files.

  1. If-else conditionals and inputs: Write a Python file that will prompt the user to input a year, and your code will print whether it is a leap year or not. (You will have to search how to use Python to input a number.)

  2. Computing \(\pi\) using numerical experiments.

    The value of \(\pi = 3.141592\) (6 decimals). How do you estimate this number? If you put a square of size \(2r\) and a circle of diameter \(2r\) in the rain and count the number of times a raindrop falls on the circle and on the square, then the ratio of drops falling on either shape will be proportional to the area of the respective shape. Thus:

    \[ \frac{\text{no. of drops on circle}}{\text{no. of drops on square}} = \frac{\pi r^2}{(2r)^2} = \frac{\pi}{4} \]

    You can watch this video for more information: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I-BC_vI4CAE.

    We can set up a numerical raindrop experiment using a random number generator in Python to compute the value of \(\pi\) using \(r=1\). Generate \(N\) random numbers for \(x\) and \(y\) between \(-1\) and \(1\). By default these points lie inside the square of side \(2\). Now for each number, check if the position \((x,y)\) lies inside the circle. If it does, then increment the counter (let's call it \(N_c\)) that keeps track of points inside the circle. For a large value of \(N\), the ratio \(\frac{N_c}{N} = \frac{\pi}{4}\). Thus \(\pi = 4 \frac{N_c}{N}\).

    Write a computer program that computes the value of \(\pi\) for a given \(N\). Then tune \(N\) such that your solution to \(\pi\) is accurate to at least 4 decimal places.

docs.title: 1.2 Basics of Animation (~3 hours)
docs.text:
Material: Watch the video and practise coding as you watch it.

https://youtu.be/NYKemmycMm4

All the code is also available for download here: Lec02_python_animations.zip

Exercise: After solving these problems, create a single zipped folder called 1b_animation.zip containing all Python files.

  1. Creating a plot:

    Consider the function \(f(v)\), where \(v\) is the velocity in m/s:

    \[ f(v) = \frac{0.25 v^2}{450 + [\log(v)]^{2.5}} - 0.023v - 9.8 \]

    Write a Python file that generates a plot of \(f(v)\) vs \(v\) for velocities from 50 to 250 m/s. Be sure to include x- and y-axis labels and an appropriate title. Use a font size of at least 21 for the title. Also ensure that the x- and y-axis tick numbers use a font size of 12 or more.

  2. Python animations:

    Create an animated face of your choice — for example, a smiling face or a crying face. At a minimum, you need to include:

    a. At least one patch object (e.g., Circle, Rectangle, Polygon).

    b. At least one moving object, using the pause() command in a loop.

    c. At least one line object, using the Line2D command.

    Here are some example faces created in my robotics course: http://youtu.be/hkML3tLI3IQ.

Continue to Part 2: Introduction to MuJoCo.

docs.title: Part 2: Introduction to MuJoCo
docs.text: For this section, you will need to install the mujoco package (see item 3 in the Equipment list).

docs.title: 2.1 Basics of modeling / XML files (~3 hours)
docs.text:
Material: Watch the video and practise coding as you watch it.

https://youtu.be/WJa-FeFRl3Q

The video uses this starter file: hello.xml

At 0:48 in the video, I show how to use the model visualizer by downloading the app. An alternate way is to type the following in the terminal inside Visual Studio Code:

python3 -m mujoco.viewer

This will bring up the model visualizer.

After completing this video, your final XML file will be: learning_xml.zip

Exercise: Your goal is to create a cascading effect like that in a Rube Goldberg machine, using geometries available in CoppeliaSim. You can also arrange different orientations/positions/sizes/shapes to create more interesting behaviors. Use at least 4 objects. Here is one example from YouTube: https://youtu.be/OHwDf8njVfo?t=85.

After solving the problem, drop the XML file in a single zipped folder called 2a_basics.zip.

Note

The source write-up says "geometries available in CoppeliaSim" here, even though this section is about MuJoCo — kept verbatim in case it's intentional (e.g. reused wording), but it reads like a leftover from an earlier version of this doc. Worth double-checking.

docs.title: 2.2 Modeling and controlling a differential drive car (~5 hours)
docs.text:
Material: Watch the videos and practise coding as you watch them.

The first video covers modeling of the differential drive car: https://youtu.be/I5QvXfo8L4o

The second video shows how to control the differential drive car: https://youtu.be/gt1fLGSggOY

The videos use this starter file: template_mujoco_python.zip

After completing the videos, your final code will be: 2D_Diff_Drive_Car.zip

Exercise: Your goal is to create a steering car and write code that enables the car to move such that it traces a figure eight, by trial and error.

After solving the problem, drop the XML and Python files in a single zipped folder called 2b_car.zip.

Continue to Part 3: Project.

docs.title: 3.1 Create your own driving game (~7 hours)
docs.text:
Material: Watch the video on creating interactive simulations and practise coding as you watch it.

https://youtu.be/KsbEuQ2iNLU

The video uses this starter file: template_mujoco_interactive.zip

After completing this video, your final code will be: 2D_projectile_game.zip

Exercise: Create a driving game where the user controls the car using the keyboard. Add features on the road such as roadblocks, other cars, etc.

After solving the problem, drop the XML and Python files in a single zipped folder called 3_project.zip.

Continue to Submission.

docs.text:
